Which detection rules should you enable first?

Our prebuilt rules now answer that with a Profile tag.
It's a points score, recalculated monthly from fleet telemetry. Full scoring model: https://t.co/eP9PFAhyIT

Additional context added via rules tags:
- Noise: alert volume per environment across the fleet 
- Performance: average and p95 execution time
- Threat: whether it covers a threat our team actively tracks 
- Profile: severity plus the other 3, rolled into Recommended or Aggressive

Profile is a quick starting point: 385 rules are Recommended.
Noise, Performance and Threat show the trade-off behind each call.
Domain, Platform and DataSource tags then narrow it to your own track.

items.content:
The user said some of his finance emails were “just disappearing.”

At first, I thought maybe he was accidentally moving them or Outlook was syncing badly.

His laptop looked clean, Defender was quiet, and there was nothing obvious running on the endpoint.

So I stopped looking at the laptop and checked the mailbox itself.

That was where I found a rule called:

RSS Feed Cleanup

The name did not look serious at all.

But when I opened the rule properly, it was looking for emails with words like:

invoice

and

payment

Then it would mark those emails as read and move them straight into the RSS Subscriptions folder.

So the messages were actually being delivered.

The user just was not seeing them in his Inbox.

I checked mailbox-level forwarding next, thinking maybe somebody was also forwarding mail outside the company.

Nothing there.

Then I checked the Microsoft 365 audit logs.

The rule had been created around 9:16 PM the previous night and modified again less than a minute later.

That was definitely not something the user remembered doing.

Now we had a different type of incident.

The attacker was not trying to destroy the mailbox.

They were trying to quietly control what the user could see.

And if you think about finance-related emails, that can become very serious very quickly.

If somebody can hide legitimate invoices or payment conversations, they can create room for fake payment instructions later without the victim seeing the original thread properly.

We disabled the rule, revoked the user’s active sessions, reset the credentials and started reviewing the sign-in history and OAuth permissions.

We also checked whether any similar rules had been created in other mailboxes.

What stood out to me here was that the laptop was not the problem.

You can rebuild the laptop completely and still miss an incident like this if the persistence or manipulation is sitting in the cloud account.

Sometimes when a user says, “My emails are disappearing,” it is worth checking more than Outlook.

Check the mailbox rules too.

That small rule can tell you a lot.

items.content:
theo here is broadly correct, but he was mostly talking about x86 virtualization, you add more software just to pretend there’s another computer, and then somehow call that security.

modern virtualization is fine and not as worse as x86 virtualization, in firecracker, kvm handles cpu and memory isolation, and vmm only exposes as little fake hardware as possible throught few virtio devices.

this reduces attack surface hugely, but firecracker still has issues, at some point a malicious packet will touch host and some magic can happen which will lead to escaping to host. or kvm might have issues that allow bypases, you are reducing still but not eliminating,

also, gvisor is pretty interesting, instead of exposing fake hardware, syscalls are intercepted and filtered, gvisor reimplements them in memory safe go, and only narrow stuff goes to host

even there, something eventually touches the host and escapes can happen.
